_doc: Hard pilot cases: long contexts (9-11 passages), near-miss numbers/versions, superseded statements, necessary-vs-sufficient traps, exceptions to general rules, world-knowledge leakage, arithmetic. Same format as spec.json; 'p' indexes into this case's passages list.
_guideline: SUPPORTED: every part entailed; allowed inference = paraphrase, counting, simple arithmetic, combining passages, version-range containment. CONTRADICTED: if the passages are true the claim must be false (wrong number/version/name for the same thing, negation, reversed comparison, always/never refuted by a stated exception). UNSUPPORTED: neither entailed nor incompatible (extrinsic facts even if true, attribute not stated for that entity, converse of an only-if, added specificity).

cases.answer: Read-only WAL databases used to be a problem: older versions of SQLite needed write access just to read a WAL-mode database. That restriction was lifted in version 3.22.0, so current versions can read a WAL database on read-only media as long as certain conditions are met, although it is still good practice to switch to journal_mode=DELETE before burning a database image onto read-only media. Large transactions were a similar story: before 3.11.0, rollback journal modes were likely to be faster for transactions over about 100 MB, but from 3.11.0 on WAL handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode. Since version 3.7.4, a process can even use WAL without shared memory, as long as it sets the locking mode to EXCLUSIVE before its first access. In WAL mode the file format version numbers in the database header are raised from 1 to 2, which is why SQLite versions older than 3.22.0 report "file is encrypted or is not a database" when they open such a file. The 3.22.0 release also made WAL the default journal mode for newly created databases.

cases.answer: SQLite has three checkpoint subtypes: PASSIVE, FULL and RESTART. Every checkpoint started with sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or by the automatic mechanism is PASSIVE, while calling sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() always produces a FULL or RESTART checkpoint. A PASSIVE checkpoint is guaranteed to run to completion as long as no other connection is writing. Because a checkpoint can only reset the WAL when no other connection is using it, a checkpoint will always reset the WAL whenever the WAL is unused. The automatic checkpoint is implemented on top of sqlite3_wal_hook() and runs in the same thread as the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit. Because of this, long-running readers never delay the automatic checkpoint.

cases.answer: By default Redis writes snapshots to a binary file called dump.rdb, and you can also take a snapshot manually with SAVE or BGSAVE: SAVE blocks the server while it runs, whereas BGSAVE does the work in a forked background child. Redis 2.4 and later will not start an AOF rewrite while an RDB snapshot is in progress, and if you call BGREWRITEAOF during a snapshot the command fails with an error, so you have to retry it once the snapshot finishes. When both AOF and RDB are enabled, Redis loads the RDB file on restart. RDB files can be copied safely while Redis is running, because a new snapshot is written under a temporary name and atomically renamed with rename(2) once it is complete. The rdbcompression option is on by default and compresses string objects with LZF.

cases.answer: In March 2026 a SQLite developer found and fixed a rare corruption bug known as the WAL-reset bug. It is likely present in every release from 3.7.0 through 3.51.2 and is fixed in 3.51.3 and later, with backports available for 3.44.6 and 3.50.6. The bug can only occur when two or more connections in separate threads or processes try to write or checkpoint at the same instant, and it affects rollback-journal databases as well as WAL databases. The developers reproduced it organically in the lab before writing the fix, and it was assigned a CVE identifier. Phil Eaton later published a reproducer that does not need the special testing code hack. Because the consequences are serious, the SQLite developers describe upgrading as an emergency.

cases.answer: To switch a running server from RDB to AOF, enable AOF on the live server with CONFIG SET appendonly yes and also update redis.conf, otherwise the change is lost when the server restarts. Redis automatically blocks incoming writes while it converts the dataset. Before restarting, wait until aof_rewrite_in_progress and aof_rewrite_scheduled are both 0. On Redis 7.0 or later, an AOF-only instance can be backed up by copying the files in the directory set by the appendfilename option, and copying them while a rewrite is running is safe. To be extra careful you can set auto-aof-rewrite-percentage to 0, which turns off automatic rewrites. If you take hard links to those files, you can re-enable rewrites before the copy finishes, because Redis only appends to files in that directory or completely replaces them. On Redis 6.0, backing up the AOF is as simple as copying the aof file, and Redis can still load the copy even if it lacks the final part.

cases.answer: With the default policy of fsync every second, Redis can lose about one second of writes in a disaster, and the fsync itself is done on a background thread; everysec has been the default since Redis 2.4. With appendfsync always, Redis still performs a separate fsync for every client write even when many writes arrive in parallel. RDB snapshots, by contrast, are usually taken every five minutes or more, so if you can live with a few minutes of data loss the docs say RDB alone is fine. With fsync disabled, AOF should be exactly as fast as RDB even under high load, but RDB can still give stronger guarantees about maximum latency under a huge write load. If the AOF ends with a truncated command, recent Redis versions refuse to start by default. Even then, the truncated file still holds a consistent point-in-time version of the dataset that, with the default policy, may be up to one second old.

cases.answer: In WAL mode writers do not block readers and readers do not block writers, so a read query against a WAL database never returns SQLITE_BUSY. If another connection has the database open in exclusive locking mode, though, all queries against it return SQLITE_BUSY; Chrome and Firefox open their database files this way, and Firefox keeps its browsing history in a SQLite file called places.sqlite. Once a connection has set EXCLUSIVE locking before its first WAL access, it can switch back with PRAGMA locking_mode=NORMAL. If the last connection crashed, the next connection to open the database runs a recovery process while holding an exclusive lock. For a database that will only be accessed by threads within a single process, a custom VFS can put the wal-index in heap memory instead of shared memory, and exclusive locking mode also makes checkpoints run faster.

cases.answer: By default the WAL is checkpointed once it reaches about 1000 pages, which is roughly 4 MB, so the default page size implied by these numbers is about 8 KB. The threshold is not fixed: it can be changed at compile time with SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT or at run time with the wal_autocheckpoint pragma. The wal-index rarely exceeds 32 KiB, which is less than 1% of a full default-sized WAL. To get the best read performance you should checkpoint as rarely as possible and let the WAL grow large. Normally the checkpoint does not truncate the WAL file unless journal_size_limit is set; instead SQLite starts overwriting the file from the beginning, because overwriting an existing file is normally faster than appending.

cases.question: What can make a SQLite WAL file keep growing, and what can an application do to keep it under control?
cases.answer: In WAL mode, SQLite normally keeps the WAL file in check by automatically checkpointing it at the end of any transaction once it exceeds 1000 pages, transferring its contents into the main database file and rewinding the WAL so new transactions start at the beginning. However, several situations can defeat this and cause unbounded growth: if the application disables or defers the automatic checkpoint mechanism through compile-time or run-time options, nothing prevents the WAL from expanding indefinitely. Checkpoint starvation is another cause, since a checkpoint can only run to completion and reset the WAL when no other connections are using it, so a database with many concurrent overlapping readers and at least one always-active reader will never let a checkpoint finish. Very large write transactions also inflate the WAL because it cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction, so a big change to a big database can produce a very large file until the transaction commits. Additionally, on SQLite versions before 3.11.0, a transaction that grows larger than the page cache could write the same page into the WAL multiple times, making the file even bigger than the logical size of the change. To keep the WAL under control, applications should leave automatic checkpointing enabled, keep read transactions short, and ensure there are "reader gaps"—times when no processes are reading from the database—so checkpoints can complete. For applications with many concurrent readers, running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option guarantees the checkpoint runs to completion before returning (and TRUNCATE also shrinks the file to zero), though the tradeoff is that readers may block while it runs. Finally, upgrading to SQLite 3.11.0 or later ensures a single transaction's WAL footprint is proportional to the transaction itself, and pragmas like wal_autocheckpoint and journal_size_limit can be used to tune the checkpoint threshold and cap the file's size on disk.

cases.question: For a production Redis deployment, should I use RDB, AOF, or both? Explain the trade-offs.
cases.answer: For most production deployments, the safest answer is to enable both persistence methods, since that combination gives you a degree of data safety comparable to what PostgreSQL provides. RDB is a compact, single-file point-in-time snapshot that is ideal for backups and disaster recovery (you can archive hourly snapshots for 24 hours and daily ones for 30 days), it allows faster restarts with large datasets, and it minimizes performance impact because the parent process only forks a child to do the disk I/O. However, RDB's main weakness is durability: since snapshots are typically taken every five minutes or more, you should be prepared to lose the latest minutes of writes if Redis crashes without a clean shutdown, and the frequent fork() calls can stall the server for milliseconds up to a second on very large datasets with weak CPUs. AOF, by contrast, is far more durable—with the default fsync-every-second policy you lose at most one second of writes while write performance remains excellent—and its append-only format resists corruption, can be repaired with redis-check-aof if a command is half-written, and even lets you recover from an accidental FLUSHALL by removing the last command from the log. The trade-offs for AOF are larger file sizes than RDB and potentially slower operation depending on the fsync policy, though with fsync disabled it matches RDB speed, and RDB still offers better maximum-latency guarantees under heavy write loads. If you care about your data but can tolerate losing a few minutes of it in a disaster, RDB alone is a reasonable choice, while AOF alone is discouraged because periodic RDB snapshots are valuable for backups, faster restarts, and protection against bugs in the AOF engine. Note that when both are enabled, Redis will use the AOF file on restart to reconstruct the dataset, since it is guaranteed to be the most complete.
